entries.label: Using the slanted side as the height
entries.description: The student puts the length of a slanted side into the area formula as the height of a trapezium or parallelogram, instead of finding the dashed height that meets the base at a right angle.

refutation.text_md: You used the slanted side as the height. That is an understandable choice: it is a number printed on the shape, and the area formula really does need a height. The catch is that the height is the dashed line, which meets the bottom edge at a right angle. The slanted side leans over, so it is a different length.

Look at the right-angled triangle on the left of the shape. Its three sides are the slanted side, the dashed height and the piece of the bottom edge up to the dashed line. The slanted side is opposite the right angle, which makes it the longest side of that triangle. So the slanted side is always longer than the height, and putting it into the formula makes the height too big.

The book finds the height first, with the theorem of Pythagoras. For the trapezium with a 15 cm slanted side and a 9 cm piece of the bottom edge: $h^{2}=15^{2}-9^{2}=144$, so $h=12$. The height is 12 cm, which is shorter than the 15 cm side you were about to use.

Now the 12 goes into the area formula: $A=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h=\frac{1}{2}(46)(12)=276\text{ cm}^{2}$. The same order works for the parallelogram with a 14 cm slanted side and an 8 cm piece of the bottom edge: $h^{2}=14^{2}-8^{2}$ gives the height, and only then do you use $A=b\times h$.

The move to use: if the shape shows a slanted side and a dashed line, but no number on the dashed line, do not use the slanted side as the height. Build the right-angled triangle, use $h^{2}=(\text{slanted side})^{2}-(\text{piece of the base})^{2}$ to find $h$, and then put $h$ into the area formula.

verdict.reason: I checked it against both canonical figures and both solutions. The error is real: the objective explicitly includes finding the height with Pythagoras first, and the labelled slanted sides (15 and 14) invite the substitution. The refutation is correct and matches the canonical working. Trapezium: h^2=15^2-9^2=144, h=12, A=1/2(16+(21+9))(12)=1/2(46)(12)=276. Parallelogram: h^2=14^2-8^2, then A=b x h. The argument is against this error, not just a restatement of the method: the slanted side is the hypotenuse of the left right-angled triangle, so it is longer than the dashed height, and the numbers show 12 < 15. The left-hand triangle is correct for both figures. No question id, page, numbered figure or review history is named; the shapes are described with their numbers. One small gap: the 46 in step 4 is not derived in this entry (entry 2 derives it). That is not wrong and not a contradiction.

entries.label: Using only part of the bottom edge as the base
entries.description: The student takes one labelled piece of the bottom edge as the base, when the bottom edge is split into pieces and the base is the whole edge with the pieces added together.

refutation.text_md: You took one of the numbers along the bottom edge as the base. That is a reasonable start: the base does lie along the bottom, and the number you picked is a real length on the shape. The catch is that the dashed line splits the bottom edge, so each number labels only a piece of it, not the whole base.

The base is the whole side from one end to the other. When the side is labelled in pieces, add the pieces first. For the parallelogram with 8 cm and 14 cm marked along the bottom, the book notes that the base is $b=8+14=22$, so the base is 22 cm, not 14 cm.

The trapezium works the same way. Its bottom edge is marked 9 cm and 21 cm, so the longer parallel side is $21+9=30$ cm. That is why the book writes $\frac{1}{2}(16+(21+9))(12)=\frac{1}{2}(46)(12)=276\text{ cm}^{2}$. Using 21 on its own would leave out the 9 cm piece, and the sum inside the brackets would no longer be 46.

The move to use: before you put numbers into the formula, add up everything labelled along the side you are using as the base, and check the total is the whole side. For the parallelogram that gives $A=b\times h$ with $b=22$ and $h=\sqrt{132}$.

verdict.reason: The error is directly supported: the canonical parallelogram solution has the note 'the length of the base is b=8+14=22', and the canonical trapezium working writes (16+(21+9)). The refutation matches both. Parallelogram: b=8+14=22 (not 14), A=b x h with h=sqrt(132). Trapezium: the longer parallel side is 21+9=30, and 16+30=46 gives 1/2(46)(12)=276. Using 21 alone gives 16+21=37, so the sum would not be 46, which is correct. The figures confirm the dashed line splits the bottom edge into labelled pieces. The refutation argues against taking a piece as the base rather than just restating the method. It uses no question ids, pages, numbered figures or review history, and its numbers are all stated in the text.

entries.label: Vertical height used for the triangular sides
entries.description: The student puts the pyramid's vertical height (straight down to the centre of the base) into $\frac{1}{2}bh$ for each triangular side, instead of the slant height measured up the side itself.
entries.signal: The triangular sides were worked with the vertical height, so the total comes out smaller than the book's.

refutation.text_md: Your plan is right: the surface area is the base plus the triangular sides, and each side is worked as $\frac{1}{2}\times b\times h$. The slip is only in which height goes in. When a pyramid shows two heights, the vertical one, the one that drops from the top point down through the inside of the pyramid, is easy to grab.

A triangular side is a flat triangle, so its height has to be measured along that side: from the bottom edge, at right angles to it, up to the top point. That is the slant height, $h_s$. The vertical height does not lie on any of the triangular sides. It runs through the inside, to the centre of the base.

The two heights are linked by the theorem of Pythagoras. In a square-based pyramid, the slant height is the longest side of a right-angled triangle whose other two sides are the vertical height and half of one side of the base. So the slant height is always longer than the vertical height. In the square pyramid with base sides $7$ and vertical height $9.36$, the slant height is $10$.

Put $9.36$ into $\frac{1}{2}bh_s$ instead of $10$, and every triangular side comes out too small. The total then falls short of $189$, because the base is unchanged and each of the four triangles has lost area it really has.

Before a height goes into $\frac{1}{2}bh_s$, check that it is the one measured along the triangular side. For this pyramid: $A=b(b+2h_s)=7(7+2(10))=189$. If only the vertical height is given, find $h_s$ first with the theorem of Pythagoras, then use $h_s$ in the areas of the triangular sides.

verdict.reason: Real error: the book's square-pyramid questions give both heights (7 / 9.36 / 10 and 4 / 8.77 / 9) and only the slant height goes into the side area. The refutation is correct throughout. The slant height is the hypotenuse of the triangle formed by the vertical height and half the base side, which matches the book's own use of Pythagoras (AF = sqrt(a^2 + h^2)). 7(7+2(10)) = 189 matches the book. Using 9.36 gives 49 + 131.04 = 180.04, which does fall short of 189. The slant height of 10 is the book's stated value, since sqrt(9.36^2 + 3.5^2) is about 9.99. It argues against this specific slip and adds nothing beyond the book's method and the LO's 'use Pythagoras where a height has to be found'. No question ids, page numbers, figure numbers or review history appear.

entries.label: Base left out of the total surface area
entries.description: The student adds up only the triangular sides of the pyramid and forgets that the base is part of the surface too.
entries.signal: The answer equals the area of the triangular sides on their own, so it falls short of the correct total by exactly the area of the base.

refutation.text_md: You found the area of the triangular sides and stopped there, as if the surface of a pyramid were only the slanted faces you see from the side. That is a natural picture, and the sides are the harder part, so that part of your work counts.
But the total surface area is every face on the outside of the solid, and the base is one of those faces. The book's method has two parts: the area of the base, plus the area of the sides.

Try it on the square-based pyramid with base sides of 7 units and a slant height of 10 units. The four triangular sides come to $4\left(\frac{1}{2}\times 7\times 10\right)=140$. The base adds $7^{2}=49$. The total is $49+140=189$ square units, which is the same as $b(b+2h_s)=7(7+2(10))=189$. Stopping at 140 would leave 49 square units of the surface uncounted.

Before you finish, check that your working has both parts. Write the base area first ($b^{2}$ for a square base), then the area of the sides, and add them: $\text{total}=\text{area of base}+\text{area of sides}$.

verdict.reason: Real error, and the omitted step is explicit in the canonical method (area of base + area of sides in we08 and ex13-7-10). The refutation's numbers are correct: 4(1/2 x 7 x 10) = 140, 7^2 = 49, total 189 = 7(7+2(10)), the book's answer for the 7/10 pyramid. It names what is left uncounted (49) and gives a concrete check (base first, then sides). It argues against the omission rather than only restating the method. The signal is exact: the answer equals the sides alone and is short by exactly the base area. No ids, pages, figure numbers or review history appear.

entries.label: Triangle area without the one half
entries.description: The student finds the area of each triangular side as base times slant height and leaves out the factor of one half, so the sides are counted twice over.
entries.signal: The answer overshoots the correct total by exactly the area of the triangular sides, as though the sides had been counted twice.

refutation.text_md: You have the right pieces: the base, plus four triangular sides, with the slant height as the height of each triangle. The slip is in the area of each triangle, where you multiplied the base by the slant height and left out the $\frac{1}{2}$.

The area of a triangle is $\frac{1}{2}bh$, and the book keeps the half in every triangular side, as in $4\left(\frac{1}{2}bh_s\right)$. Without the half you have found $bh_s$, which is twice the area of the triangle.

Check it on the square-based pyramid with base sides of 4 units and a slant height of 9 units. Each triangular side is $\frac{1}{2}\times 4\times 9=18$, so the four sides come to $4(18)=72$, and with the base $4^{2}=16$ the total is $16+72=88$ square units. Without the half, each side would be $4\times 9=36$ and the four sides $144$, twice the $72$ they really cover, and the total would wrongly be $160$.
Write each triangular side as $\frac{1}{2}\times b\times h_s$ before you multiply by the number of sides, so the half is in the working from the start, then add the base.

verdict.reason: Real error, and the canonical solutions keep the 1/2 in every triangular side (3(1/2 x b x h_s) in we08, 4(1/2 b h_s) in ex13-7-10). The refutation is arithmetically correct and consistent with the book. For the 4/9 pyramid each side is 18, the four sides are 72, the total is 16 + 72 = 88 (the book's answer), and without the half each side is 36, the sides are 144 and the total is 160. The statement that 144 is twice the 72 the sides really cover is correct. It targets this slip specifically and adds nothing beyond the book. The signal is exact: the overshoot equals the area of the sides, 160 - 88 = 72. No ids, pages, figure numbers or review history appear.

entries.label: Leaves out the circular base
entries.description: The student finds only the area of the walls, $\pi r\times$ slant height, and gives it as the total surface area, forgetting the circular base.
entries.signal: The answer is $\pi r$ times the slant height, with no $\pi r^2$ term added.

refutation.text_md: You found the area of the walls, and $\pi r\times$ slant height is the right way to do that. The question asks for the total surface area, though, and a cone has two surfaces, not one: the walls and the circular base underneath.

The book builds the total from both: surface area $=$ area of the base $+$ area of the walls. Take a cone with radius 4 and slant height 10. The base is $\pi\times 4^2 = 16\pi$ and the walls are $\pi\times 4\times 10 = 40\pi$.
The book's total is $16\pi + 40\pi = 56\pi$. An answer that stops at $40\pi$ is short by exactly the base, $16\pi$, so it describes the walls only, not the whole cone.

So for a total surface area, always add the base: $\pi r^2 + \pi r\times(\text{slant height})$, which the book also writes as $\pi r(r + \text{slant height})$. Before you choose, check that your calculation has both a base part and a walls part.

verdict.reason: The error is real for this objective, since the book defines total surface area as base plus walls. The refutation is correct and uses the canonical pieces: base pi*4^2 = 16pi, walls pi*4*10 = 40pi, total 56pi, which matches the cone with r=4 and slant height 10 in the canonical solution. It also gives the factored form pi r(r + slant height). It argues against this specific slip (stopping at the walls and being short by exactly the base). It uses no question ids, page numbers or figure numbers, and no review history. The cone is stated in full numbers.

entries.label: Writes the walls as $2\pi r\times$ slant height
entries.description: The student uses the slant height correctly but writes the area of the walls with an extra factor of 2, as $2\pi r\times$ slant height, instead of $\pi r\times$ slant height.
entries.signal: The total is $\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\times$ slant height, so the walls come out exactly twice as big as they should.

refutation.text_md: You have the right pieces: the base is $\pi r^2$, and you put the slant height into the walls where it belongs. The slip is the extra 2. The walls of a cone are $\pi r\times$ slant height, not $2\pi r\times$ slant height.
Here is where the book gets the walls. Open them out flat and cut the curved surface into many thin triangles whose height is close to the slant height. Together their bases add up to $2\pi r$.

Each triangle has area $\tfrac{1}{2}\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$, so all of them together give $\tfrac{1}{2}\times 2\pi r\times(\text{slant height}) = \pi r\times(\text{slant height})$. The $\tfrac{1}{2}$ cancels the 2, so no 2 is left in the walls.

Check it on the book's cone with radius 4 and slant height 10. The walls are $\pi\times 4\times 10 = 40\pi$ and the total is $16\pi + 40\pi = 56\pi$. With the extra 2 the walls would be $80\pi$ and the total $96\pi$, far above the book's $56\pi$.
Use $\pi r\times(\text{slant height})$ for the walls and add $\pi r^2$ for the base: $\pi r^2 + \pi r\times(\text{slant height})$.

verdict.reason: The refutation follows the book's derivation: thin triangles with height about equal to the slant height, whose bases sum to 2 pi r, giving (1/2) x 2 pi r x slant height = pi r x slant height. The arithmetic checks out: with the extra 2 the walls would be 80pi and the total 96pi, against the correct 56pi. It targets the doubled factor specifically and does not just restate the formula. It teaches nothing beyond the book's derivation and contains no forbidden references.

entries.label: Uses the vertical height instead of the slant height
entries.description: The student puts the vertical height of the cone into the walls' formula $\pi r\times$ height, instead of the slant height measured along the side of the cone.
entries.signal: The total is $\pi r^2 + \pi r\times(\text{vertical height})$, so it comes out smaller than the correct total.

refutation.text_md: You have the right plan: $\pi r^2$ for the base and $\pi r\times(\text{height})$ for the walls. The slip is which height. You used the vertical height, straight down from the top of the cone to the centre of the base. The walls slope, so the book measures them along the slant height, from the top down the side of the cone to the edge of the base.

The vertical height, the radius and the slant height make a right-angled triangle. The vertical height and the radius are the two shorter sides, meeting at the right angle at the centre of the base, and the slant height is the longest side. So the slant height is always longer than the vertical height, and using the vertical height makes the walls too small.

The book's cone with radius 4 and vertical height 14 shows how this works. The book first finds the slant height with the theorem of Pythagoras: $\sqrt{4^2 + 14^2} = \sqrt{212} = 2\sqrt{53}$. The walls are then $\pi\times 4\times 2\sqrt{53} = 8\pi\sqrt{53}$ and the total is $16\pi + 8\pi\sqrt{53} = 233.2\ \text{cm}^2$. Using 14 for the walls would give $16\pi + 56\pi = 72\pi$, about $226.2$, which is too small.

When a question gives both heights, as in the book's cone with radius 4, vertical height 9.16 and slant height 10, the walls use the slant height $10$. When only the vertical height is given, find the slant height first with $\sqrt{r^2 + (\text{vertical height})^2}$. Then use $\pi r^2 + \pi r\times(\text{slant height})$.

verdict.reason: All the maths checks against the figures and canonical solutions. For r=4 and vertical height 14, the slant height is sqrt(212) = 2 sqrt 53, the walls are 8 pi sqrt 53 and the total is 233.2 cm^2. Using 14 gives 16pi + 56pi = 72pi, about 226.2, which is smaller. The right triangle with the vertical height and radius as legs and the slant height as hypotenuse is correct, so the slant height is the longest side. The case where both heights are given (r=4, vertical height 9.16, slant height 10) uses the slant height 10, as the canonical solution does. The advice to find the slant height from sqrt(r^2 + h^2) when only the vertical height is given matches the worked example. It argues against this specific error and has no forbidden references.

entries.label: Slant height used as the height
entries.description: The student puts the slant height (the length along the slanting side of the cone or pyramid) into the volume formula where the vertical height $H$ belongs.
entries.signal: The volume comes out too big, because a slanting length is longer than the straight-up height. For example, a square pyramid with base side 8 units, vertical height 8 units and slant height 8.94 units gives 190.72 instead of 170.67.

refutation.text_md: You have the right formula and you have put in a real length from the question, which is good. The slip is which length. The slant height runs down along the side of the cone or pyramid, but the formula needs the vertical height $H$: the length that goes straight up from the base to the top.
The slant height leans over, so it is always longer than the vertical height. Using it makes the solid look taller than it really is, so the volume comes out too big.

Take a square pyramid with base side 8 units, vertical height $H=8$ units and slant height 8.94 units. With the vertical height, $V=\frac{1}{3}b^{2}H=\frac{1}{3}(8)^{2}(8)=\frac{512}{3}\approx 170.67$ units$^3$. Putting in 8.94 instead gives $\frac{1}{3}(8)^{2}(8.94)=190.72$ units$^3$, which is too big.

Sometimes the question gives the slant height and no vertical height. Then the radius, the vertical height and the slant height make a right-angled triangle, with the slant height as the longest side, and Pythagoras gives $H$. For a cone with radius 5 cm and slant height 13 cm: $H^{2}=13^{2}-5^{2}=144$, so $H=12$ cm, and $V=\frac{1}{3}\pi(5)^{2}(12)=100\pi\approx 314.2$ cm$^3$.

Next time, before you substitute, ask which length goes straight up from the base. If the question gives it as $H$, use it and leave the slant height unused. If it is missing, find it with Pythagoras first, then put $H$ into the formula.

verdict.reason: The error is real here: the book's cone and pyramid questions deliberately give a slant height (7.28, 8.94, 8.60, 8.73) alongside H and then ignore it, and two questions (13 cm/5 cm cone, 20 cm/12 cm cone) require Pythagoras to turn the slant height into H. I checked the figures. 8.94, 7.28, 8.60 and 8.73 are the slant lengths along the face or side, and the vertical H is the dashed perpendicular. All the arithmetic in the refutation is correct: (1/3)(64)(8)=512/3≈170.67; (1/3)(64)(8.94)=190.72, which is too big; 13²−5²=144 so H=12, and V=100π≈314.2. These match the canonical answers. The method is the book's own (V=(1/3)b²H, cone V=(1/3)πr²H, H found by Pythagoras). The claim that the slant height is longer than H is true, since it is the hypotenuse. The refutation argues against the specific slip and does not just restate the method. It names no question id, page number, figure number or review history. The signal (volume too big, 190.72 vs 170.67) is accurate.

entries.label: Whole sphere's volume used for a half sphere
entries.description: The student puts the full sphere volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ in for a solid that is only half a sphere, such as a half scoop of ice-cream, and never halves it.
entries.signal: A half-sphere volume that is exactly double the correct one, for example 113.1 cm³ for a half scoop of radius 3 cm instead of 56.5 cm³.

refutation.text_md: You used the formula for a whole sphere, $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, and that part is right: it is the sphere formula. The catch is that this solid is only half a sphere, so the formula gives you twice the volume you need.

Take a half scoop of ice-cream with radius $3$ cm. A whole sphere of radius $3$ cm has volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi(3)^3=36\pi\approx 113.1$ cm$^3$. The book's working says the volume of a half sphere is half the volume of a sphere, so the half scoop is only half of that.
So the scoop is $\frac{4}{3}\pi(3)^3\times\frac{1}{2}=18\pi\approx 56.5$ cm$^3$, not $113.1$ cm$^3$.

See what the doubling does to the comparison. The cone with radius $3$ cm and height $12$ cm holds $\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(12)=36\pi\approx 113.1$ cm$^3$. With the whole sphere's $113.1$ cm$^3$ the ice-cream would look exactly as big as the cone. The real scoop is $56.5$ cm$^3$, which is less than $113.1$ cm$^3$, so the melted ice-cream fits.
Next time you meet a half sphere, write $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\times\frac{1}{2}$, the whole-sphere formula times one half, then substitute $r$ and calculate.

verdict.reason: The error is real and supported. The book's ice-cream question uses a half scoop and says its volume is half the volume of a sphere, and the half-sphere teaching item uses V=(4/3)πr³×1/2. The refutation's numbers all match the canonical solution: the whole sphere with r=3 gives (4/3)π·27=36π≈113.1; the half scoop is 18π≈56.5; the cone (1/3)π·9·12=36π≈113.1. The comparison step is also correct. The doubled value would equal the cone's volume, while the true scoop of 56.5 is less than 113.1, so the ice-cream fits, which is the book's conclusion (A: Yes). It does not wrongly claim the doubled value would flip the answer. The method is the book's (sphere formula times 1/2). The refutation argues against the specific slip (using the whole-sphere formula for a hemisphere) and does not merely restate the method. The wording 'the book's working' is a general mention and not a question id, page, figure number or review reference. The signal (exactly double, 113.1 vs 56.5) is accurate and specific to this error.

entries.label: Counts the faces where the two solids meet
entries.description: The student finds the full surface area of each solid and adds them, so the face the pyramid sits on and the pyramid's own base are counted even though both are covered.
entries.signal: A total surface area larger than the exposed-faces total by the area of the face where the solids meet, or by twice that area.

refutation.text_md: You found the full surface area of each solid and added the two totals. Finding each solid's area is the right start, and so is adding. The catch is that two of the faces you counted are not on the outside of the finished solid.

Where the pyramid sits on the cube or prism, the pyramid's base is covered by the solid beneath it, and the face it sits on is covered by the pyramid. Nobody can see or touch either face, so neither is an exposed face, and the total surface area counts only the exposed faces.

Try a cube of side $5$ $\text{cm}$ with a square pyramid on top. Counting everything gives the cube's six faces, $6\times25=150$, plus the pyramid's base, $25$, plus its four triangles, $65$: that is $240$ $\text{cm}^2$. Counting only the exposed faces gives five faces of the cube, $5\times25=125$, plus the four triangles, $65$: that is $190$ $\text{cm}^2$. The extra $50$ $\text{cm}^2$ is exactly the two covered faces, $25$ each.

So before you add, ask which faces are covered. For the solid underneath, count every face except the one the pyramid sits on. For the pyramid, count only its slanted triangular faces and leave out its base. Then add the areas of those exposed faces.

verdict.reason: The error is real here. The book's worked example (cube with a square pyramid) states that one cube face and the pyramid's base are covered, so only 5 cube faces and 4 triangles count. Its worked example with the triangular prism also uses only the prism base, the prism sides and the exposed pyramid faces. I re-checked the refutation's numbers: 6x25=150, plus 25, plus 65 gives 240; 5x25=125 plus 65 gives 190; the difference is 50, which is two covered faces of 25 each. The 190 total matches the book's answer for the 5 cm cube with the 6 cm pyramid, and the 65 is 4 x 16.25 from slant height 6.5. The steps contain no question ids, page numbers, figure references or review history. The method taught (exclude the covered face and the pyramid's base, add the exposed faces) is the canonical one. The refutation argues against the specific mistake rather than just restating the method. The signal (total too large by one or two covered-face areas) would not misdiagnose a student. Minor weakness: the 65 for the triangles is not derived in the text, but it is correct.

entries.label: Uses the whole height of the solid as the pyramid's height
entries.description: Given the overall height of the composite solid, the student puts that number in as the height of the pyramid instead of subtracting the height of the cube or prism underneath it.

refutation.text_md: You used the height given for the whole solid as the height of the pyramid. The formula you chose, $\frac{1}{3}\times\text{base}\times H$, is the right one for the pyramid. What needs another look is the number you put in for $H$.

The height of the pyramid is measured from its base up to its tip, and the pyramid is only the top part of the solid. The overall height starts at the bottom of the whole solid, so it also includes the height of the cube or prism underneath.

Take a cube of side $7$ $\text{cm}$ with a square pyramid on top, and the whole solid is $22$ $\text{cm}$ tall. The pyramid's height is $22-7=15$ $\text{cm}$, so its volume is $\frac{1}{3}(7)^2(15)=245$ $\text{cm}^3$, and with the cube the total is $343+245=588$ $\text{cm}^3$. Using $22$ instead gives about $359.3$ $\text{cm}^3$ for the pyramid, which counts the cube's $7$ $\text{cm}$ of height a second time.

So subtract first: height of the pyramid $=$ overall height $-$ height of the cube or prism. Use that height in $\frac{1}{3}\times\text{base}\times H$, and in the theorem of Pythagoras if you need the slant height, then add the volumes.

verdict.reason: The error is real and well supported. In the book's cube-and-pyramid examples the overall height is given (11 cm with a 5 cm cube; 22 cm with a 7 cm cube), and the pyramid's height must be found by subtraction (6 and 15 cm). I re-checked the refutation's arithmetic: pyramid height 22-7=15; (1/3)(49)(15)=245; 343+245=588, which matches the canonical answer 588; (1/3)(49)(22)=359.33, so 'about 359.3' is right. It uses the book's own formula and method, mentions Pythagoras only generically for the slant height, and cites no question id, page, figure or review history. It argues against the specific mistake of using the whole height, not just the method. It has no signal, so there is nothing to misdiagnose.

entries.label: Uses the vertical height where the slant height belongs
entries.description: The student puts the vertical height of the cone or pyramid straight into the surface area formula in place of the slant height, so the sloping surface is measured with a length that is too short.
entries.signal: For a cone with radius 3 cm and vertical height 10 cm, the answer comes out as about $122.52\text{ cm}^2$ (that is $39\pi$) instead of $126.67\text{ cm}^2$.

refutation.text_md: You put the vertical height (the length that goes straight up through the middle of the solid) into the surface area formula where the slant height belongs. Your formula is the right one, and both lengths are called a height, so it is an easy swap to make.

They are different lengths. The vertical height runs straight up inside the solid, from the middle of the base to the top. The slant height runs along the sloping surface, from the top down to the edge of the base. Together with the radius of the base they make a right-angled triangle, and the slant height is its longest side, so it is always longer than the vertical height.

Take a cone with radius $3\text{ cm}$ and vertical height $10\text{ cm}$. Using $10$ as the slant height gives $\pi(3)(3+10)=39\pi\approx 122.52\text{ cm}^2$. The real slant height is $h_s=\sqrt{3^2+10^2}=\sqrt{109}\approx 10.44\text{ cm}$, and $\pi(3)(3+\sqrt{109})\approx 126.67\text{ cm}^2$. The first answer is too small because the surface slopes for $10.44\text{ cm}$, not $10\text{ cm}$.

A square pyramid works the same way, with one thing to watch. The vertical height lands in the middle of the base, so the other short side of the right-angled triangle is half of the base side, not the whole side. For a base side of $15\text{ cm}$ that short side is $7.5\text{ cm}$, and you use $h_s^2=(7.5)^2+h^2$.

So first ask what the length you were given is. If it is marked along the sloping side, it already is the slant height and you can use it straight away. If it is the vertical height, find the slant height first with the theorem of Pythagoras ($h_s^2=r^2+h^2$ for a cone), then put $h_s$ into the surface area formula: $\pi r(r+h_s)$ for a cone, or $b(b+2h_s)$ for a square pyramid, where $b$ is the whole base side.

verdict.reason: The error is real for this objective and supported by the canonical solutions. In the worked cone example the book finds the slant height first, with h_s = sqrt(3^2+10^2) = sqrt(109), and only then uses pi*r*(r+h_s) = 126.67 cm^2. The cone figure confirms r = 3 and a dashed vertical height of 10. The refutation's numbers check out: pi*3*(3+10) = 39*pi = 122.52, and sqrt(109) = 10.44, giving 126.67. The square-pyramid step matches the book's method too. The figure shows a 15 cm base and a 12 cm vertical height, the book uses (7.5)^2 + 12^2 for the slant height, and b(b+2h_s) is the book's formula with b the whole base side. The advice 'if marked along the sloping side, use it directly' agrees with the book's other cone example, where 20 cm along the slope goes straight into the surface-area formula. The refutation argues against the swap itself, giving the geometric reason (the slant height is the hypotenuse) and a numeric contrast, rather than just restating the method. It teaches only Pythagoras, the book's own tool. The label, description, signal and steps cite no question ids, pages, figures or review history. One side note for whoever owns the canonical: the book's final pyramid figure of 437.26 does not match its own formula, which gives about 649.5. The refutation never states a pyramid area, so it does not conflict with it.

entries.label: Volume grows by only $k$ when the radius is scaled
entries.description: The student expects the volume to be multiplied by $k$ whenever any one dimension is multiplied by $k$, so for a cylinder whose radius is multiplied by $k$ they write $kV$ instead of $k^2V$, often by turning $\pi(kr)^2$ into $\pi kr^2$.
entries.signal: The new volume of a cylinder whose radius is multiplied by $k$ is given as $kV$ (or $\pi kr^2h$) rather than $k^2V$.

refutation.text_md: You have spotted something true: when the height of a prism is multiplied by $k$, the volume is multiplied by $k$ too, because the new volume is $l\times b\times(kh)=kV$. The slip is carrying that pattern over to the radius, where it does not hold.

The height works that way because it appears in the volume formula once, as a single factor. The radius is different. In $V=\pi r^2\times h$ it appears squared, so the new radius $kr$ has to go in as $(kr)^2$.
The square applies to the whole of $kr$, not just to $r$: $(kr)^2=kr\times kr=k^2r^2$. Writing $\pi kr^2$ leaves out one of the two factors of $k$.
So the new volume is $V_n=\pi(kr)^2\times h=\pi k^2r^2\times h=k^2\times\pi r^2h=k^2V$. With $k=2$, doubling the radius makes the volume 4 times as big, not 2 times.

Next time, write the new dimension in brackets, for example $(kr)$, and put it into the original formula exactly where the old one stood. Expand the brackets, then group what is left as the original volume $V$. The factor in front of $V$ is your answer.

verdict.reason: The error is real for this objective. we19 shows the height scaling the volume by k, and a student can wrongly carry that over to the radius in we20, writing pi*k*r^2*h for pi*(kr)^2*h. Every step of the refutation checks out against we20: (kr)^2 = k^2 r^2, V_n = pi(kr)^2 h = k^2 V, and the k=2 case gives 4 times the volume. Step 1 matches we19's l*b*(kh) = kV. The argument is aimed at this slip, namely the single-factor pattern and the unsquared k, not just a restatement of the method. It uses no different method and teaches nothing outside the book. It cites no question id, page, figure or review history. The signal (kV or pi*k*r^2*h instead of k^2 V) would not misdiagnose a student. No options or predicates are attached.

entries.label: Scales the whole surface area by one factor
entries.description: When the radius of a cylinder is multiplied by $k$, the student multiplies the whole surface area by a single factor, $k$ or $k^2$, instead of finding how each term of the area formula changes.
entries.signal: The new surface area of a cylinder whose radius is multiplied by $k$ is given as $kA$ or $k^2A$.

refutation.text_md: Scaling the area as one block is a natural move, because the volume really does change by a single factor ($k^2V$ when the radius is multiplied by $k$). The surface area is not like that: it is a sum of terms, and they do not all change by the same factor.
Start from $A=\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ and put in the new radius $kr$, leaving $h$ alone: $A_n=\pi(kr)^2+2\pi(kr)h=\pi k^2r^2+2\pi krh$.
Now look at the $k$'s one term at a time. The first term has $k^2$, because $r$ is squared in it. The second has only $k$, because $r$ appears once in it. So $A_n=k^2(\pi r^2)+k(2\pi rh)$.

No single factor can match this. With $k=2$ the first term is multiplied by 4 and the second by 2. Multiplying the whole area by 4 would make the second term twice what it should be, and multiplying the whole area by 2 would make the first term half what it should be.
So put the new dimension into every term of the area formula, then collect the $k$'s term by term. Don't try to attach one factor to the whole area.

verdict.reason: The error is real and is supported by we20. The canonical A_n = k^2(pi r^2) + k(2 pi r h) is a term-by-term result with different factors, so a single factor k or k^2 on the whole area is a genuine wrong move. The refutation follows the canonical steps exactly: it starts from A = pi r^2 + 2 pi r h, substitutes kr, and collects k^2 on the first term and k on the second. The k=2 check is correct. Multiplying the whole area by 4 would double the second term, and multiplying it by 2 would halve the first. Step 1 correctly says the volume does scale by one factor, k^2 V. It cites no question id, page, figure or review history, and the signal (kA or k^2 A) is accurate. No options or predicates are attached. One note for upstream: the canonical formula A = pi r^2 + 2 pi r h has only one end disk, while the we20 figure shows a closed cylinder, which would give 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h. The refutation is faithful to the canonical solution, which is the authority, and its conclusion holds either way, so I am confirming it.

The book's cylinder surface-area formula is $A=\pi r^2+2\pi rh$, with a single $\pi r^2$ term. The surface-area refutation follows it exactly and never says which faces the terms stand for. A reviewer may want to confirm this is the book's intended surface.

The worked solution for the cylinder with a scaled radius stops at $A_n=k^2(\pi r^2)+k(2\pi rh)$ and prints no closing sentence. The surface-area refutation does not go beyond that expression. It does not solve any scaling of the height for surface area, because the book does not solve it.

entries.label: Multiplies the area or volume by k itself
entries.description: The student treats the scale factor as acting directly on the area, surface area or volume, so doubling every length is taken to double the area (or a quarter of every length to make a quarter of the area).
entries.signal: The answer is the scale factor itself: 2 for the surface area of a cone whose radius and height are doubled, 4 for the volume of a prism whose sides are quadrupled, $\frac{1}{3}$ for a circle whose radius becomes a third, $\frac{1}{4}$ for a square whose sides become a quarter.

refutation.text_md: You are thinking that if every length is multiplied by $k$, the area (or volume) is multiplied by $k$ as well. That is true for a length, and finding $k$ from the wording is the first real step, so that part is fine. The slip is that area and volume are not lengths.

An area is built from two lengths multiplied together, so the factor gets applied twice. Take a circle whose radius becomes a third of its size: $A_{\text{new}}=\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}r\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{9}\pi r^{2}=\frac{1}{9}A$. The new area is $\frac{1}{9}$ of the original, not $\frac{1}{3}$.

The same thing happens with a square whose sides are each a quarter of the original: $A_{\text{new}}=\left(\frac{1}{4}s\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{16}s^{2}=\frac{1}{16}A$. Check it with numbers: a square of side 4 has area 16, and a square of side 1 has area 1, which is $\frac{1}{16}$ of 16, not $\frac{1}{4}$.
A volume is built from three lengths, so the factor is applied three times. When the sides of a triangular prism are quadrupled, $k=4$ and the volume is multiplied by $4^{3}=64$, not by 4.
So after you have found $k$ from the words ("doubled" gives $k=2$, "quadrupled" gives $k=4$), do not stop there. For an area or surface area, work out $k^{2}$. For a volume, work out $k^{3}$.

covers.text: The scale factor was applied once (k), not squared (k²) — a linear length scaling used for an area

I checked each worked figure against the canonical answers: circle with radius a third gives 1/9, square with side a quarter gives 1/16, prism with sides quadrupled gives 64, cone with radius and height doubled gives 4. The signal values (2, 4, 1/3, 1/4) are exactly the unsquared or uncubed k for those questions. The refutation argues against the slip, not just the method. entries.label: Uses the wrong power of k for what is being asked
entries.description: The student chooses $k^{2}$ or $k^{3}$ by the kind of shape instead of by the quantity asked for, typically cubing $k$ for the surface area of a solid or squaring $k$ for a volume.
entries.signal: A surface area answer of $k^{3}$ (8 for a cone whose radius and height are doubled), or a volume answer of $k^{2}$ (16 for a triangular prism whose sides are quadrupled).

refutation.text_md: You know the factor has to be raised to a power, and you have found $k$. The slip is in which power: it depends on what you are asked for (area or volume), not on whether the shape is flat or solid. A cone is a solid, but its surface area is still an area.

The book's rule: when every dimension is multiplied by $k$, an area (including a surface area) is multiplied by $k^{2}$, and a volume is multiplied by $k^{3}$. Surface area is measured in square units and volume in cubic units.

The book puts both on one solid. A prism has volume $493\ \text{cm}^{3}$ and surface area $6007\ \text{cm}^{2}$, and every dimension is multiplied by 4. The volume becomes $493\times4^{3}=31\,552\ \text{cm}^{3}$ and the surface area becomes $6007\times4^{2}=96\,112\ \text{cm}^{2}$. It is the same solid and the same $k$, with two different powers.

Now compare the two answers for a doubled cone and a quadrupled prism. Doubling the cone's radius and height multiplies its surface area by $2^{2}=4$, not by $2^{3}=8$. Quadrupling the sides of a triangular prism multiplies its volume by $4^{3}=64$, not by $4^{2}=16$.
Before you square or cube $k$, ask "is this asking for an area or a volume?" Use $k^{2}$ for surface area and area, and $k^{3}$ for volume.

verdict.reason: The error is real: choosing k^3 for a surface area or k^2 for a volume. It is directly contrasted by the canonical answers (cone surface area 4, prism volume 64) and by the book's single-prism example, which uses 4^3 for the volume and 4^2 for the surface area. I recomputed 493x64=31 552 and 6007x16=96 112; both are correct. The cone (2^2=4, not 8) and prism (4^3=64, not 16) conclusions match the canonical solutions. The signal values 8 and 16 are the right diagnostics. The refutation targets the slip: it is the quantity asked for, not the shape, that sets the power. It uses only the book's rule and units. The phrases "the book's rule" and "the book puts both on one solid" are generic, restate all the numbers, and give no id, page or figure number. No attachments.

entries.label: Uses k = 3 when a length becomes a third
entries.description: The student reads "a third of its original size" (or a quarter, or half) as a factor of 3 (or 4, or 2) instead of $\frac{1}{3}$, so a shape that gets smaller is given a larger area or volume.
entries.signal: A whole number greater than 1, such as 9 or 16, as the answer to a question in which every length gets smaller, for example 9 for a circle whose radius becomes a third.

refutation.text_md: Your method is right: square $k$ for an area and cube it for a volume. What has flipped is $k$ itself: "a third of its original size" has been read as 3 instead of $\frac{1}{3}$.

$k$ is the number you multiply each original length by to get the new length. A radius that becomes a third of its size is $\frac{1}{3}r$, so $k=\frac{1}{3}$. With $k=3$ the radius would be three times as long as it was.

A quick check is whether the shape gets bigger or smaller. If every length shrinks, the area and the volume must shrink too. Squaring $k=3$ gives 9, which says the circle's area grew ninefold, and that cannot be right for a smaller circle. With $k=\frac{1}{3}$: $A_{\text{new}}=\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}r\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{9}\pi r^{2}$, one ninth of the original.

The same applies to the other cases: sides that are a quarter of the size give $k=\frac{1}{4}$ and a new area of $\frac{1}{16}$ of the original, and a radius and height that are both halved give $k=\frac{1}{2}$ and a volume of $\frac{1}{8}$ of the original.

Start by writing down what each length is multiplied by ("doubled" is 2, "a quarter of its size" is $\frac{1}{4}$). Check whether the shape grows or shrinks, then use $k^{2}$ for an area or $k^{3}$ for a volume. The answer should be bigger than 1 only if the shape got bigger.

verdict.reason: The error is real: reading a third, a quarter or a half as 3, 4 or 2. It is supported by the canonical items for a circle radius a third (1/9), a square side a quarter (1/16) and a cylinder radius and height halved (1/8). The refutation grants the correct method (k^2 or k^3) and attacks only the misreading of k. Every number checks: (1/3)^2=1/9, (1/4)^2=1/16, (1/2)^3=1/8. The grows-or-shrinks sanity check is consistent with the book's answers and adds no new method. It avoids the book's cone-formula slip in the cylinder item and still states the correct 1/8. No ids, pages, figure numbers or review history appear. The signal (a whole number above 1 when everything shrinks, such as 9 or 16) would not misdiagnose a student.
